exam_traps.why: No prevention is perfect, so detection is essential to find what gets through. A sound program needs both.

key_terms.definition: A control that tells people what to do, such as a policy or a sign; some sources list it as a separate function.
Automatically switching to a backup system when the main one fails.

subtopics.name: Layering and Compensating Controls
subtopics.definition: Layering means protecting an asset with several controls of different types and functions, so that when one fails, others still protect it and gaps can be covered.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every control can fail or be bypassed. Mixing technical, administrative and physical controls means one mistake, such as a stolen password, does not lead straight to a breach.
how_it_works: Cover each important risk with more than one type, such as a policy, a technical block and a physical lock.
Mix functions, so a failure of prevention is still detected and corrected.
When the required control is not possible, a compensating control reduces the same risk another way, with documented approval.
A compensating control should reduce the risk about as well as the control it replaces, and be reviewed regularly.
Domain 4 covers defense in depth further as a network design idea.
subtopics.example: A factory's old machine controller cannot run antivirus or MFA, and replacing it would halt production. A security analyst helps plan compensating controls: an isolated network segment, one approved maintenance laptop, a locked cabinet and a weekly review of its access logs. The plant manager, who owns the system, approves them as a documented exception.

review: Test whether each substitute actually blocks or detects the original threat
Inspect the exception record for owner approval and a review date
evidence: Exception record listing the missing control and its substitutes
Logs or tests showing the compensating controls work
audit_focus.recommend: Document missing controls and proposed substitutes for the system owner's approval.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves compensating controls and accepts what remains

subtopics.isaca_rule: Never rely on one control. When the standard control cannot be used, document why and add compensating controls that reduce the same risk, approved by the system owner.

exam_traps.trap: If the required control cannot be installed, accept the risk and move on.
exam_traps.why: First look for compensating controls that reduce the same risk another way. Any acceptance still belongs to the owner, not the practitioner.

exam_traps.trap: Adding more controls of the same kind gives layered protection.
exam_traps.why: Two firewalls with the same rules can fail the same way. Real layering mixes types and functions so one weakness does not defeat them all.

key_terms.definition: Layering independent controls so that one failure does not expose the asset.
Older technology still in use that may not support modern security features or updates.

subtopics.name: Controls for AI Tools
subtopics.definition: AI tools need the same three control types as any other system: technical, administrative and physical safeguards that protect their data, models and actions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI systems handle sensitive data and can act automatically, so a control gap can leak data or let a poisoned or tricked model cause harm at scale.
how_it_works: Technical: restrict who can change models and training data, filter inputs and outputs, and log prompts and actions.
Administrative: an AI use policy, a risk review before deployment, human review of high-impact outputs and staff training.
Physical: secure the data centers, servers and hardware where models and training data are kept.
AI agents get least-privilege accounts, so a manipulated agent can do only limited harm.
Monitoring watches for unusual model behavior, which can signal poisoning or misuse.
subtopics.example: An insurance company uses an AI assistant that drafts claim decisions. A security analyst lists its controls by type: a technical permission so the assistant can only read claim files, an administrative rule that a claims officer approves every decision, and physical protection of the servers in the locked data center. Noticing that prompts are not logged, they raise it with the system owner.

review: Confirm the AI agent's permissions cover only its task
Inspect whether prompts and AI actions are logged and kept
evidence: Permission list for the AI service account
Sample of AI decision records with human approvals
audit_focus.recommend: Report AI tools lacking logging or human review to the AI system owner.
audit_focus.decides: The AI system owner decides deployment and accepts remaining risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify AI controls the same way as any others: technical, administrative, physical. Keep a person accountable for high-impact AI decisions, and limit and log what AI agents can do.

exam_traps.trap: AI tools need only technical controls because they are software.
exam_traps.why: They also need administrative controls, such as policy, approval and human review, and physical protection of the hardware and data they run on.

exam_traps.trap: Human review is unnecessary once a model tests as accurate.
exam_traps.why: Models can drift, be poisoned or be tricked by crafted input. Human oversight of high-impact decisions catches errors that testing missed.

key_terms.definition: A design where a person reviews or approves an AI system's output before it takes effect.
A decline in a model's accuracy over time as real-world data changes.

topics.overview: This topic covers how a security professional is expected to behave: following a code of conduct, showing due care and due diligence, and living by the ISC2 Code of Ethics. It also covers reasoning through ethical dilemmas, how the code is enforced, and ethical use of AI at work.
can_do: Tell due care from due diligence in a scenario
State the four ISC2 canons in order and apply all of them to a dilemma
Choose the action that protects the public while staying honest and legal
Identify who may file an ethics complaint under each canon

subtopics.name: Professional Code of Conduct
subtopics.definition: A professional code of conduct is a written set of expected behaviors, from an employer or professional body, covering honesty, conflicts of interest, confidentiality and lawful conduct.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security staff hold powerful access and sensitive knowledge. A code makes expectations clear, protects the people the organization serves and gives a basis for action when someone crosses the line.
how_it_works: Employers publish codes of conduct that staff accept, often alongside the acceptable use policy.
Professional bodies, such as ISC2, have their own codes that members must follow to keep their certification.
Common themes are honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest, protecting confidential information and obeying the law.
Security staff use their access only for assigned work, never out of curiosity.
Concerns go through proper channels, such as a manager, an ethics hotline or the legal team.
subtopics.example: A database administrator at a hospital hears that a well-known local figure has been admitted. Coworkers ask them to look up the diagnosis, since they have access. They refuse, because their access exists only for assigned work, and they report the request to the privacy officer as the hospital's code of conduct requires.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Access is a trust, not a perk. Use it only for assigned work, avoid conflicts of interest, keep confidences and raise concerns through proper channels rather than handling them privately.

exam_traps.trap: Looking at records out of curiosity is harmless if you have access and change nothing.
exam_traps.why: Having access is not the same as having a reason. Viewing records without a work need breaches confidentiality, privacy rules and the code of conduct.

exam_traps.trap: A professional body's code replaces the employer's code of conduct.
exam_traps.why: Both apply. Professionals follow their employer's code and their professional code, and raise any conflict between them instead of silently picking one.

key_terms.definition: A situation where personal interests could improperly sway professional decisions, such as assessing a vendor you own shares in.
A channel, often anonymous, for reporting suspected misconduct without going through a direct manager.

subtopics.name: Due Care and Due Diligence
subtopics.definition: Due diligence is doing the homework to understand risks and check that safeguards work; due care is acting on that knowledge by taking the reasonable steps a prudent person would.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Courts, regulators and customers judge organizations by whether they acted reasonably. Falling short on either can count as negligence, even where no law named the specific control.
how_it_works: Due diligence investigates: researching a vendor, assessing risks, testing controls and keeping up with threats.
Due care acts: patching known flaws, enforcing policy, training staff and fixing what diligence uncovered.
Both are ongoing; diligence keeps checking, and care keeps acting on what the checks find.
The test is what a reasonable, informed professional would have done in the same situation.
Failing to take reasonable care when harm was foreseeable can be judged negligence.

rows.label: Core idea
cells: Do: act responsibly on what you know

rows.label: Example
cells: Reviewing a cloud vendor's security reports before signing
Requiring MFA after learning staff accounts are being phished

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Did we find out what we should have known?
Did we do what a reasonable person would do?

subtopics.example: Before a city council signs with a payroll provider, a security analyst reviews the provider's independent security report and finds weak backup practices: due diligence. The council then makes tested backups a contract requirement before signing: due care. The analyst also schedules yearly re-checks, which continue the diligence, and records each step for the contract owner.

review: Confirm vendor reviews happen before contracts and on a schedule
Trace earlier findings to the actions taken to fix them
evidence: Vendor security review records with dates
Remediation tickets closed for previously found issues
audit_focus.recommend: Report findings with no follow-up action to the owner as a gap in due care.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides the reasonable level of protection

subtopics.isaca_rule: Diligence is finding out; care is acting on what you found. A scenario that researches, assesses or verifies points to due diligence; one that implements, enforces or fixes points to due care.

exam_traps.trap: Due diligence is done once, before signing a contract.
exam_traps.why: Diligence continues. Risks and vendors change, so monitoring and re-checking are part of it.

exam_traps.trap: Knowing about a risk is enough to show due care.
exam_traps.why: Knowledge without action is exactly the gap negligence claims target. Due care means taking reasonable steps on what diligence found.

key_terms.definition: The standard that asks what a reasonable, careful person with similar knowledge would have done in the situation.
Failing to take the care a reasonable person would take, leading to foreseeable harm.

subtopics.memory_aid: Diligence discovers; care carries it out.

subtopics.name: The ISC2 Code of Ethics
subtopics.definition: The ISC2 Code of Ethics is the set of mandatory principles every ISC2-certified member agrees to follow, made up of a preamble and four canons.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Following the code is a condition of certification. A breach can lead to a complaint, a review and loss of the credential, and ethics scenarios are a recurring exam theme.
how_it_works: The preamble says members must hold high ethical standards so they protect public safety, serve their principals well and treat each other with respect.
Canon 1: Protect society, the common good, public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
Canon 2: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally.
Canon 3: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
Canon 4: Advance and protect the profession.
subtopics.example: A newly certified analyst at a payments company is asked by a friend at a rival firm for a copy of their employer's internal incident response playbook, just as a starting point. Handing it over without permission would breach their duty to their employer (canon 3) and be dishonest toward it (canon 2). They decline and point the friend to public NIST incident response guidance instead.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Know the four canons in order and what each protects: the public, honest and legal conduct, principals, and the profession. Treat the code as binding, not aspirational; certification depends on it.

exam_traps.trap: The code is voluntary guidance for good behavior.
exam_traps.why: Agreeing to the code is a condition of ISC2 certification. A proven breach can lead to sanctions, including losing the credential.

exam_traps.trap: Principals means only the company's leadership.
exam_traps.why: Principals are those you serve professionally, such as employers and clients. Canon 3 asks for diligent, competent service to them.

key_terms.definition: Anyone a professional serves under an agreement, such as an employer or client.
One of the four core rules of the ISC2 Code of Ethics.
The opening statement of the code, explaining its purpose before the canons.

subtopics.memory_aid: In order: society, honor, principals, profession.

subtopics.name: Applying the Canons to Dilemmas
subtopics.definition: Applying the canons means testing each possible action against all four of them and choosing one that protects the public while staying honest, legal and responsible to principals.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Real dilemmas pit loyalty to an employer against public safety or honesty. The code gives a structured way to think, but ISC2 gives no rule for ranking the canons, so judgment is needed.
how_it_works: List the options, then ask of each: does it harm the public, break the law or require dishonesty?
Reject any option that is illegal or deceptive, even if an employer asks for it.
The best option usually satisfies several canons at once, such as reporting a safety issue through official channels.
Use proper channels and stay within your authority; never take vigilante action such as hacking back.
The code supports your own ethical judgment; it does not replace it.
subtopics.example: A security engineer at a medical device maker finds that an infusion pump's wireless link lets anyone change doses. Their manager says to stay quiet until the next product release. The engineer documents the flaw and escalates it to the product security lead and the compliance team, pressing for patient warnings, because silence would leave patients at risk and mislead customers.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the action you could defend to the public, a regulator and your employer at once: honest, legal, protective of people and done through proper channels. Never pick an answer just because its canon is listed first; check all four.

exam_traps.trap: Loyalty to the employer means keeping a flaw quiet when told to.
exam_traps.why: Canon 3 asks for diligent service to principals, not concealment that leaves the public at risk or requires dishonesty. Escalate through proper channels.

exam_traps.trap: Canon 1 is listed first, so it settles every conflict on its own.
exam_traps.why: ISC2 lists the canons in order but gives no ranking rule. Weigh the whole situation; the best answer usually honors several canons together.

key_terms.definition: Reporting serious wrongdoing to authorities or regulators, often after internal channels fail; many laws protect people who do.
Attacking an attacker's systems in return; usually illegal and contrary to professional ethics.

subtopics.name: Ethics Complaints and Enforcement
subtopics.definition: ISC2 enforces its code through a formal complaint process, in which a written, sworn complaint is reviewed by an ethics committee and may lead to sanctions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The process shows the code has real consequences, and it sets out who may raise which concerns, a detail that can appear in exam scenarios.
how_it_works: Complaints are written and sworn, and should name the canon the complainant believes was broken.
Anyone may complain under canons 1 and 2; only principals, such as employers or clients, under canon 3.
Under canon 4, only other certified or licensed professionals who follow an ethics code may complain.
The committee does not investigate on its own; it weighs the evidence submitted and acts only when there is a solid initial case.
The ISC2 board decides any sanction, which can include revoking certification.
subtopics.example: A project manager believes a certified contractor falsely reported finishing a security test. As the client who hired the contractor, the manager can complain under canon 3 as well as canon 2. They write and swear the complaint, name both canons and attach the test records as evidence.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The code is enforced, not just admired. Match the concern to the canon and to who has standing: anyone for canons 1 and 2, principals for canon 3, fellow professionals for canon 4.

exam_traps.trap: Any member of the public can file a complaint under any canon.
exam_traps.why: Standing depends on the canon. Anyone may cite canons 1 and 2, but canon 3 complaints come from principals and canon 4 complaints from fellow professionals.

exam_traps.trap: The ethics committee investigates every rumor about a member.
exam_traps.why: The committee does not investigate on its own. It reviews sworn complaints and the evidence submitted, and closes those without a solid initial case.

key_terms.definition: The right to bring a complaint, based on your relationship to the matter.
A written statement the writer formally swears is true.

subtopics.name: Ethical Use of AI at Work
subtopics.definition: Ethical AI use means applying the same honesty, care and respect for people's data to AI tools as to any other work, with a person answerable for the results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI makes it easy to share confidential data, pass off unchecked output as expert work or act on wrong answers. The canons still apply, and accountability stays with the professional.
how_it_works: Keep principals' confidential data out of AI tools not approved for it, as the canons and privacy law expect.
Check AI output before relying on it; competent service means verifying, not just pasting.
Be honest about AI's role where it matters, such as in reports, and never present guesses as verified findings.
Never use AI to deceive, impersonate or harm, such as writing phishing emails outside an authorized test.
Report AI behavior that could harm the public, such as a model leaking personal data, through proper channels.
subtopics.example: A junior analyst at a consulting firm uses an approved AI assistant to summarize a client's scan results. The summary says a server is fully patched, but the raw data shows a critical patch is missing. The analyst corrects the report before sending it and tells their lead, since passing on unchecked AI output would fail the client.
subtopics.isaca_rule: AI is a tool; the professional stays accountable. Protect principals' data, verify output before relying on it, be honest about how work was produced, and use AI only within your authorization.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI made the mistake, the analyst is not responsible.
exam_traps.why: The professional who relies on the output owns the result. Diligent, competent service means checking AI work before it reaches a client or a decision.

exam_traps.trap: Using AI to write a convincing phishing email is fine if it is only practice.
exam_traps.why: Creating attack content is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test, such as a sanctioned phishing exercise. Otherwise it risks real harm and breaks the law and the code.

key_terms.definition: AI output that sounds confident but is false or made up.
AI-generated audio, image or video that imitates a real person, often used to deceive.

key_terminologies.CIA triad: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three core goals of security.
key_terminologies.AAA: Authentication, authorization and accounting: prove identity, grant permissions, record activity.
key_terminologies.Non-repudiation: Proof strong enough that a person cannot credibly deny an action, usually from a digital signature.
key_terminologies.Personally identifiable information (PII: Data that identifies a person, alone or combined with other data.
key_terminologies.Privacy by design: Building privacy protections into a system from the first design step, with protective defaults.
key_terminologies.Threat: Anything that could harm an asset, such as an attacker, an error or a storm.
key_terminologies.Vulnerability: A weakness a threat can exploit, such as unpatched software.
key_terminologies.Risk: The likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability, combined with the impact if it does.
key_terminologies.Risk treatment: Responding to a risk by avoiding, mitigating, transferring or accepting it.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk left after controls are applied.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The broad amount and type of risk leaders will take on to meet goals.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The narrower, measurable limit of risk accepted for a specific objective.
key_terminologies.Risk owner: The person with authority to decide a risk's treatment and accept what remains.
key_terminologies.Annualized loss expectancy (ALE): Expected yearly loss from a risk: single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence.
key_terminologies.Regulation: A mandatory rule issued by a government agency under the authority of a law.
key_terminologies.Framework: A published, usually voluntary structure for building a security program, such as NIST CSF 2.0.
key_terminologies.Policy: A mandatory, high-level statement of what is required and why, approved by senior management.
key_terminologies.Standard: A mandatory, specific requirement that supports a policy, such as approved encryption settings.
key_terminologies.Procedure: Mandatory step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task.
key_terminologies.Guideline: Optional, recommended practice that leaves room for judgment.
key_terminologies.Technical control: A safeguard built into hardware or software, such as a firewall or encryption.
key_terminologies.Administrative control: A policy, procedure, training or people practice that directs behavior.
key_terminologies.Physical control: A tangible safeguard for people and facilities, such as a lock, fence or guard.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control that lowers the same risk when the usual control is not possible.
key_terminologies.Due diligence: Investigating and verifying: finding out what risks exist and whether safeguards work.
key_terminologies.Due care: Acting responsibly on what you know, as a reasonable person would.
key_terminologies.ISC2 Code of Ethics: The preamble and four canons every ISC2-certified member must follow.
key_terminologies.Model or data poisoning: Corrupting an AI model or its training data so it learns wrong or hidden behavior; an integrity attack.
